name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
monetization: Manufactures nearly all leading-edge AI silicon (Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom XPUs, Apple) and owns the CoWoS advanced-packaging capacity that paces the entire buildout.
description_md: TSMC is the dominant leading-edge contract chipmaker: N5/N3 in volume, N2 ramping, with 7nm-and-below nodes now 77% of wafer revenue. Its high-performance-computing (HPC) platform — AI accelerators, data-center silicon, GPUs — is 66% of revenue. Critically, TSMC also owns CoWoS advanced packaging, the single most-cited chokepoint of the AI buildout: every Nvidia Blackwell/Rubin part and most custom ASICs must transit it. Fabs are concentrated in Taiwan, with Arizona expanding under a US investment program raised to $265B.
ai_monetization_md: Wafer and advanced-packaging revenue from effectively every AI chip designer: Nvidia (wafers + ~60% of 2026 CoWoS capacity), AMD, Broadcom/Google TPUs, Apple, and the custom-ASIC wave. AI demand converted directly into pricing power and record profitability — Q2 2026 revenue of $40.2B (+36% y/y) at a record 67.7% gross margin — and into a capex step-up to $60–64B for 2026. Because CoWoS capacity allocations determine who can ship accelerators, TSMC effectively rations the industry's output; capacity is being scaled toward ~130–150K wafers/month by late 2026.
ai_strategy_md: Stay 2+ nodes ahead (N2 in ramp, A16 next) so that AI compute has no substitute supplier; double CoWoS capacity for the Rubin generation rather than let packaging cap customers' roadmaps; expand geographically under customer and government pressure (additional $100B pledged to Arizona in July 2026, total US commitment $265B) while keeping leading-edge R&D in Taiwan. Management raised 2026 revenue growth guidance to slightly above 40%, citing AI demand it describes as structural rather than cyclical.
risk_notes_md: **Concentration both ways:** Nvidia alone books ~60% of 2026 CoWoS output; conversely every AI roadmap on earth depends on one company's packaging lines — a single point of failure the bottleneck registry tracks explicitly. **Geopolitics:** Taiwan concentration is the systemic tail risk; US fabs carry higher costs. **Cycle risk:** the 2026 capex step-up ($60–64B) is justified by AI orders whose end-funding is contested; a demand fall would strand new CoWoS/N2 capacity. **China:** export controls bar leading-edge sales into China, and TSMC has halted advanced supply to Chinese AI-chip designers.

observations.notes: +36% y/y; record gross margin 67.7%; Q3 guide $44.6–45.8B; 2026 growth outlook raised to >40%.
HPC (AI accelerators, DC silicon, GPUs) grew 20% q/q; smartphone fell to ~22% of revenue.
Guided range $60–64B, raised at least $4B above the prior forecast; midpoint shown. Heavily weighted to leading-edge and CoWoS expansion.

events.title: Q2 2026: record quarter; 2026 growth raised to >40%, capex to $60–64B, US investment to $265B
events.why_it_matters: The single best real-time gauge of whether AI capex is converting into paid silicon — record revenue/margins plus a raised capex plan signal TSMC sees the order book as durable. An extra $100B was pledged to Arizona.

events.title: Nvidia books over half of 2026–27 CoWoS capacity
events.why_it_matters: Formalizes the packaging chokepoint: competitors' 2026 accelerator volumes are residual claims on whatever CoWoS Nvidia didn't take, pushing overflow to ASE and others.
